posts.title: TXA does not make a clot. It stops the one you already have from dissolving.
posts.text:
TXA does not make a clot. It stops the one you already have from dissolving.

Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue. It occupies the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, so plasminogen and plasmin cannot bind fibrin. Clot lysis is inhibited. The drug is not pro-thrombotic in itself; it stabilizes clot that has already formed rather than generating new clot. That mechanism is why the entry's trauma regimen reads the way it does: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h, started within 3 hours of injury. It is also why the first clinical pearl is the clock. After 3 hours, CRASH-2 showed increased bleeding-related death. Two more lines from the full-detail entry: infuse the loading dose over at least 10 minutes, because a push drops the pressure, and do not run it in the same line as blood products or penicillins.

Open the tranexamic acid entry and read its clinical pearls.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

posts.title: HR 118, SBP 92. Divide the first by the second before you call it borderline.
posts.text:
HR 118, SBP 92. Divide the first by the second before you call it borderline.

Shock index is heart rate over systolic blood pressure. SI = HR / SBP. For this patient, 118 / 92 = 1.28. The calculator labels that result High, significant shock, consider MTP. The bands it uses: below 0.5 low-normal, 0.5 to under 0.7 normal, 0.7 to 1.0 elevated with possible hypovolemia, above 1.0 high. A pulse of 118 is tachycardic. A systolic of 92 sits just above the SBP <90 trauma criterion on the MTP card. The ratio says more than either value, which is why the Massive Transfusion Protocol card lists a shock index above 1.0 among its clinical activation signs. The source behind the calculator is Allgöwer and Burri, 1967. Tag the triage nurse who already does this division in their head.

Run your own numbers in the Shock Index calculator.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

#TenetrixInsight #TriageNurse #EmergencyNursing #ClinicalCalculators
posts.first_comment_text: Calculator shock_index (statref://calculators/shock_index): SI = HR / SBP, source Allgöwer M, Burri C. Schockindex. Dtsch Med Wochenschr 1967. Bands as coded: <0.5 low-normal, 0.5 to <0.7 normal, 0.7–1.0 elevated (possible hypovolemia), >1.0 high (consider MTP). The MTP card (statref://card/massive-transfusion-protocol) lists 'Shock index >1.0 (HR/SBP)' under clinical signs and 'SBP <90 despite fluids' under trauma criteria for activation.

posts.title: Four collared patients, GCS 15, stable vitals. One leaves without imaging. Which?
posts.text:
Four collared patients, GCS 15, stable vitals. One leaves without imaging. Which?

All four are alert blunt-trauma patients, aged 16 or over, seen within 48 hours, systolic at or above 90 and breathing 10 to 24 a minute, so the Canadian C-Spine Rule applies. A: 68 years old, ground-level fall, no deficits, no midline tenderness. B: 30 years old, simple rear-end collision, walked at the scene, no midline tenderness, actively turns the head 45 degrees each way. C: 24 years old, dove head-first into shallow water, neck pain only. D: 40 years old, tripped on a curb, immediate neck pain, midline tenderness, has not sat up or walked since. Which one reaches NO RADIOGRAPHY on the algorithm, and which rule question stops each of the others? Answer and the three questions in the first comment.

Comment A, B, C or D, then check the flowchart on the Cervical Spine Clearance card.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

#TenetrixInsight #CSpine #EmergencyMedicine #TraumaNursing
posts.first_comment_text: B. Question 1, high-risk factors (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, paraesthesias in the extremities): A is 68, so radiography; C is an axial load to the head (diving), so radiography. Question 2, a low-risk factor must be present before range of motion is tested (simple rear-end MVC, sitting in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed-onset neck pain, absence of midline tenderness): D has none, so radiography, because it is not safe to test rotation. B has low-risk factors and, at Question 3, actively rotates 45° left and right, so NO RADIOGRAPHY. The endpoint card quotes the derivation: sensitivity 100 %, specificity 42.5 % (Stiell 2001, n = 8,924); validation CCR 99.4 % vs NEXUS 90.7 % (Stiell 2003). Algorithm cards ccr-entry, ccr-high, ccr-low, ccr-rotate, ccr-no-xr, ccr-xr on statref://card/msk-cervical-spine-clearance.

posts.title: Crash Responder Safety Week. MARCH reorders the survey: hemorrhage first, airway second.
posts.text:
Crash Responder Safety Week. MARCH reorders the survey: hemorrhage first, airway second.

Move Over or Slow Down is this week's message for drivers passing a crash scene. MARCH is the tactical trauma survey; the card lists it for penetrating or blast trauma, prehospital combat casualty care and mass-casualty triage, and it puts massive hemorrhage ahead of the airway. One letter per slide. M, massive hemorrhage: control life-threatening external bleeding first; tourniquet high and tight for extremities, wound packing and direct pressure for junctional wounds. A, airway: chin lift or jaw thrust, nasopharyngeal airway, recovery position. R, respiration: needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, vented chest seal. C, circulation: reassess hemorrhage control, IV or IO access, permissive hypotension, TXA within 3 h, blood products for shock. H, hypothermia and head: remove wet clothing, insulate, warm fluids. The card explains the order: exsanguination is the leading cause of preventable death on the battlefield, which is why MARCH diverges from civilian ABC. What does your rig carry for M?

Tell us in the comments what your service stocks for M, then open the MARCH card.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

posts.title: The lowest GCS is 3, not 0. Motor (1–__) is the term missing from the formula.
posts.text:
The lowest GCS is 3, not 0. Motor (1–__) is the term missing from the formula.

Formula Friday. The formula line on the calculator reads GCS = Eye (1–4) + Verbal (1–5) + Motor (1–__); range 3–15. The three components as the app lists them. Eye opening: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none. Verbal response: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none. Motor response is the third component, and its top score is the blank. The lowest possible total is 3, not 0, because every component scores at least 1. The calculator's bands: 13 and above mild impairment, 9 to 12 moderate, 8 or below severe, consider definitive airway. Source: Teasdale and Jennett, Lancet 1974. Put the missing maximum in the comments. The answer is pinned in the first comment.

Comment the number, then open the GCS calculator and score a patient from memory.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

posts.first_comment_text: 6. Motor response as the calculator lists it: 6 obeys commands, 5 localizes pain, 4 withdraws from pain, 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate), 2 extension (decerebrate), 1 none. Caliper legs on two R waves read 800 ms. Every strip this winter starts from this one.

This strip is the baseline every strip this winter gets compared against. Regular. A P wave before every QRS. The caliper tool is on: press and drag across the trace and the readout gives the interval in ms, in small boxes, in seconds, and as a rate if the span is one R to R. Name the rhythm and the rate; the answer is in the first comment.

posts.title: The MTP card's bottom line: activate on clinical judgement, never on a hemoglobin.
posts.text:
The MTP card's bottom line: activate on clinical judgement, never on a hemoglobin.

The Hemorrhagic Shock / Massive Transfusion bundle gathers the set: the MTP card, Trauma Assessment, the TXA and calcium chloride entries, and Tuesday's shock index. Keep: 1:1:1 pRBC to FFP to platelets; pack 1 is 6 units pRBC, 6 units FFP, 1 apheresis platelets; calcium 1 to 2 g IV per 4 units pRBC; lethal triad is temperature under 35 °C, pH under 7.2, coagulopathy. Score it: Revised Trauma Score for GCS 10, SBP 80, RR 32 returns 5.88, moderate mortality risk. November is National Diabetes Month; the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State bundle is under Endocrine / Metabolic on the Conditions list. It is also National Family Caregivers Month, for the people caring for someone at home. Next week: breathing and oxygen, and ventilation is not oxygenation.

Open the Hemorrhagic Shock / Massive Transfusion bundle before week two starts.

posts.text:
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min: roughly 44% FiO2. Non-rebreather at 15: up to 95%.

Flow rate is not FiO2. From the card Oxygen Delivery Devices: Nasal cannula, 1–6 L/min: FiO2 about 20% + (4% × L/min), so 24% at 1 L and 44% at 6. Simple face mask, 5–10 L/min, 35–50%, never below 5 L/min or the patient rebreathes CO2. Venturi, fixed 24, 28, 31, 35, 40 or 50% by adapter. Non-rebreather, 10–15 L/min, 60–95%, and the reservoir bag must stay inflated. High-flow nasal cannula, up to 60 L/min, 21–100%, with dead-space washout and a mild PEEP effect. Every one of these changes the oxygen going in. None of them tells you whether CO2 is coming out. That is this week's mechanism: ventilation is not oxygenation. The last slide is the Breathing and oxygen module, whose Foundations lessons walk the same path from air to tissue. Foundations is an optional one-time purchase. Swipe, then save this for the next time you chart it.

posts.title: DKA with potassium under 3.3 mEq/L: the insulin waits. The entry says why.
posts.text:
DKA with potassium under 3.3 mEq/L: the insulin waits. The entry says why.

The full-detail entry for REGULAR INSULIN (IV) states the mechanism: it binds the insulin receptor, drives glucose uptake, suppresses gluconeogenesis, halts lipolysis and therefore ketogenesis, and drives potassium into cells through the Na+/K+-ATPase. That is why potassium moves with the glucose. The entry's monitoring lines: glucose hourly on an infusion; potassium every 2–4 hours, because it will fall as insulin drives it intracellularly even when the initial value was high. And the capitalised contraindication: DKA with potassium under 3.3 mEq/L means replace potassium first. Hyperkalemia dose as listed: 10 units IV with 25 g dextrose. Save this for the next time you chart it.

posts.title: PaO2 100 on 40% oxygen is a P/F of 250. The respiratory rate had no vote.
posts.text:
PaO2 100 on 40% oxygen is a P/F of 250. The respiratory rate had no vote.

The P/F ratio answers one question only: how well oxygen is crossing into the blood for the oxygen you are giving. Formula as the calculator prints it: P/F = PaO2 / FiO2 (FiO2 as a decimal). Worked example on screen: PaO2 100 mmHg on 40% oxygen. 100 / 0.40 = 250. The app labels the result by the Berlin severity bands: 300 and above normal oxygenation, 200 to 299 mild, 100 to 199 moderate, below 100 severe. So 250 falls in the mild band (Berlin also requires PEEP of at least 5 cmH2O, bilateral opacities and onset within a week before the word ARDS applies), and the respiratory rate had no vote. The ventilation side has its own calculator, Minute Ventilation: MV = (Tidal Volume × Respiratory Rate) / 1000, so 450 mL × 14 = 6.3 L/min, normal range 4 to 10. Two numbers, two separate failures. Tag the RT who taught you the difference.

Tag the RT, then open the calculator in Tenetrix Insight, link in bio.

posts.title: Type I is an oxygen problem. Type II is a CO2 problem. The fixes are not interchangeable.
posts.text:
Type I is an oxygen problem. Type II is a CO2 problem. The fixes are not interchangeable.

From the card Respiratory Failure Types, four lines.
Type I, hypoxemic: PaO2 under 60 mmHg on room air with PaCO2 normal or low; mechanism V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion impairment.
Type II, hypercapnic: PaCO2 over 45 mmHg; mechanism alveolar hypoventilation.
BiPAP helps Type II because it augments ventilation; it does not treat Type I on its own.
Do not over-oxygenate chronic CO2 retainers.
The card also carries Types III and IV, the acute-versus-chronic table and the indications for intubation. Veterans Day: to the veterans on shift today, and the ones who trained the rest of us, thank you. Save this for the next time you chart it.

posts.title: Four new infiltrates, four admission clocks. Only one of them is HAP.
posts.text:
Four new infiltrates, four admission clocks. Only one of them is HAP.

Four patients, one diagnosis label. Which one is hospital-acquired pneumonia by the card's definition?
A. New infiltrate and fever 20 hours after admission.
B. New infiltrate 52 hours after admission, never intubated.
C. Infiltrate on the chest film in the ED, intubated an hour later.
D. Infiltrate 30 hours after admission in a patient who took antibiotics last month.
Only one of these crosses the line the card draws, and the line is a number of hours. The answer, the number, and what changes about the empiric regimen are in the first comment. Put the letter below.

A (20 h) and D (30 h) fall short of 48 hours; D's antibiotics in the last 90 days are an MDR risk factor, not a definition. C presented on arrival. 52 hours is also early-onset on the card (under 5 days, less resistant organisms). What changes: the HAP card's low-MDR-risk options include levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily, cefepime 2 g IV q8h or piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h, and high MDR risk adds antipseudomonal cover (cefepime, pip-tazo or meropenem) plus MRSA cover (vancomycin or linezolid). posts.title: Grunting is an infant building its own PEEP. Seven other signs sit beside it on the card.
posts.text:
Grunting is an infant building its own PEEP. Seven other signs sit beside it on the card.

World Pneumonia Day falls on a Thursday this year. The card Pediatric Respiratory Distress lists eight signs: tachypnea above the normal rate for age; retractions, subcostal, intercostal or suprasternal; nasal flaring; grunting, an expiratory sound the card explains as the infant creating its own PEEP; head bobbing from accessory muscle use; cyanosis, perioral or central, a late sign; stridor, inspiratory and therefore upper airway; wheezing, expiratory and therefore lower airway. The lines that follow are the ones to read twice: decreased work of breathing is paradoxically ominous, and bradycardia is a late sign. Target SpO2 as the card states: 92% or above, 90% with chronic lung disease. Question for the comments: which of the eight do you usually notice first from the doorway?

posts.first_comment_text: From the card Community-Acquired Pneumonia (statref://card/pneumonia-cap). Outpatient, healthy: amoxicillin 1 g TID or doxycycline 100 mg BID, 5–7-day course; with comorbidities: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 BID + azithromycin 500 mg/250 mg; alternative: levofloxacin 750 mg daily. Inpatient non-ICU, standard: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO daily; alternative: levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily; minimum 5 days, until afebrile 48–72 hours. ICU, severe CAP: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Quick cards: CEFTRIAXONE (statref://drug/ceftriaxone) — do not mix with calcium-containing IV solutions. AZITHROMYCIN (statref://drug/azithromycin-iv) — QT prolongation, avoid in QTc over 500 ms. LEVOFLOXACIN (statref://drug/levofloxacin) — FDA black box: tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects; QT prolongation. DOXYCYCLINE (statref://drug/doxycycline) — photosensitivity; avoid in pregnancy and children under 8. Card sources: IDSA/ATS CAP guidelines 2019.

posts.title: Room air, PaO2 90, PaCO2 40: an A–a gradient of 9.7. One constant is blank.
posts.text:
Room air, PaO2 90, PaCO2 40: an A–a gradient of 9.7. One constant is blank.

Formula Friday. This week's formula is the alveolar gas equation, as the A–a Gradient calculator prints it, with one term blanked:
A–a = [(FiO2 × 713) − (PaCO2 / ___)] − PaO2
Fill the blank and say what the constant stands for. On screen: FiO2 0.21, PaO2 90, PaCO2 40, no age entered, result 9.7 mmHg against an expected 15. The calculator adjusts the expected value when you enter an age. It labels a gradient just above expected as mildly elevated, and one 15 mmHg or more above expected as V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion defect, which is the Type I column from Wednesday's card. The answer and the arithmetic are in the first comment.

Fill the blank in the comments, then check it in Tenetrix Insight, link in bio.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

#TenetrixInsight #FormulaFriday #ABG #RespiratoryTherapy
posts.first_comment_text: 0.8 — the respiratory quotient. The calculator's source line reads: standard alveolar gas equation (sea level, RQ 0.8). The arithmetic on screen: 0.21 × 713 = 149.7; 40 / 0.8 = 50; 149.7 − 50 = 99.7; 99.7 − 90 = 9.7 mmHg. Expected with no age entered is 15; with an age it is age / 4 + 4. statref://calculators/aa_gradient

posts.title: Regular is the insulin the card clears for IV. Roll NPH, never shake it.
posts.text:
Regular is the insulin the card clears for IV. Roll NPH, never shake it.

Weekend read for World Diabetes Day: one card and one bundle. The card Insulin Types & Dosing, four lines. Rapid-acting: onset 15 minutes, peak 1 hour, duration 2–4 hours, given with the meal tray present. Regular: onset 30 minutes, peak 2–3 hours, duration 3–6 hours, the one the card lists for IV use in DKA and HHS. NPH: onset 2–4 hours, peak 4–12, duration 12–18, cloudy, roll do not shake, never IV. Long-acting: no peak, 20–24 hours, never mixed. Then the Hypoglycemia bundle, which gathers the treatment card and two drugs, D50W and glucagon, on one screen. Inside the card: the Rule of 15, Level 1 at 54–70 mg/dL and Level 2 below 54, and glucagon's onset of 10–20 minutes.

posts.title: Urticaria is absent in up to 20% of anaphylaxis. Do not wait for it.
posts.text:
Urticaria is absent in up to 20% of anaphylaxis. Do not wait for it.

The Anaphylaxis bundle puts the card Anaphylaxis Management beside its five drugs, epinephrine first. The lines to keep: epinephrine IM is first-line, 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000) in the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5–15 minutes. The card's criteria: skin or mucosal signs plus respiratory distress, hypotension or end-organ dysfunction, or hypotension, bronchospasm or laryngeal obstruction alone, rapidly after a known or likely allergen. Laryngeal edema carries the highest mortality risk. The adjuncts are not substitutes for epinephrine. Observe 4–6 hours minimum for the biphasic reaction. Today is the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims; thank you to the crews on those scenes. Next week: how much oxygen the blood is actually carrying. Save this for the next time you chart it.
